newsitem.title: CHINA: China lashes U.S. over Hong Kong and human rights.
newsitem.headline: China lashes U.S. over Hong Kong and human rights.

text.p: Beijing on Thursday lashed out at the United States over Hong Kong and human rights, accusing Washington of Cold War thinking and saying ignorant U.S. congressmen were trying to meddle in China's internal affairs.

In a double diplomatic barrage, the State Council, or cabinet, and a Foreign Ministry spokesman both accused the United States of using spurious concerns to interfere in issues that concerned China alone.

The U.S. House of Representatives had wronged China on Tuesday when it approved a bill that called on Beijing to honour its promises on Hong Kong, spokesman Cui Tiankai told a news briefing in Beijing.
The bill calls on China to honour its treaty with Britain which promises Hong Kong extensive autonomy after its return to to Chinese rule on July 1.
"There are some people in the U.S. Congress who know nothing about realities in Hong Kong and have no idea about China's Hong Kong policy," Cui said.
"This kind of gross interference in China's internal affairs is wrong," he said. "We are resolutely opposed to this and definitely cannot accept it."

An annual report by the U.S. State Department that criticised China for widespread human rights abuses and the crushing of almost all political dissent was a slanderous attempt to provoke confrontation, the State Council said.
"This is a full manifestation of the stubborn Cold War mentality of the United States," it said in a commentary issued by the official Xinhua news agency.

"The annual human rights 'reports' of the U.S. State Department have therefore become an important tool for opposing China, vilifying China, and interfering in the internal affairs of China," it said.
Sino-U.S. relations have long been strained by disputes over issues ranging from human rights and trade to Taiwan, but both sides have made great efforts to strengthen ties in recent months.

U.S. Vice President Al Gore is scheduled to become the most senior American to visit China in eight years when he arrives in Beijing later this month for meetings intended to help pave the way for an exchange of presidential visits.

The Sino-U.S. rapprochement has already had to withstand friction over alleged Chinese funding of U.S. politicians, and analysts say Hong Kong is likely to become a new diplomatic minefield as the handover nears.

The U.S. House of Representatives' bill, approved by a 416-1 vote, declared that failure to ensure an elected legislature for Hong Kong would violate a 1984 agreement with Britain and called on China to honour its treaty obligations.
China has vowed to scrap the British colony's current elected legislature and replace it with its own appointed body.
Beijing also plans to roll back legislation introduced by Britain to protect human rights, prompting protests from London and pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong.
While Hong Kong is a relatively new source of contention in Sino-U.S ties, human rights are an almost perennial issue.

Washington was ignoring China's efforts to improve the lives of its people, the State Council said in its long and bitter commentary, which also dismissed U.S. criticism of Beijing's curbs on freedom of speech.

Human rights activists have long criticised Beijing for its rigid supression of political dissent and its tight control on the uniformly state-controlled media, but the commentary said China's policies complied with international practice.
"In fact, U.S. law limits the freedom of speech, press and information in a more severe way," it said.
